paragraphs: And Shorten the Terms of Leases

What I have said about servants and masters applies, to a certain extent, to landowners and tenant farmers, but this subject deserves to be considered separately. In America there are, properly speaking, no tenant farmers; every man owns the ground he works. It must be admitted that democratic laws greatly tend to increase the number of landowners and to reduce the number of tenants. Yet what happens in the United States owes much less to the country’s institutions than to the country itself. In America land is cheap, so anyone can easily become a landowner; its returns are small, so its produce cannot well be divided between a landowner and a farmer. In this, as in many other respects, America therefore stands alone, and it would be a mistake to take it as an example.

I believe that in democratic countries, as in aristocratic ones, there will be landowners and tenants, but the connection between them will be of a different kind. In aristocracies the hire of a farm is paid to the landlord not only in rent but in respect, regard, and duty; in democracies all of it is paid in cash. When estates are divided and pass from hand to hand, and the lasting connection that once existed between families and the soil is dissolved, landowner and tenant come into contact only by chance. They meet for a moment to settle the terms of the agreement, then lose sight of each other. They are two strangers brought together by a common interest, who bargain keenly over a business matter whose sole object is to make money.

As property is subdivided and wealth spreads across the country, the community fills with people whose former opulence is declining, and with others whose fortunes are of recent growth and whose wants increase faster than their resources. For all of these people the smallest money profit matters, and none of them is inclined to give up any of his claims or to lose any part of his income. As ranks intermingle, and as very large fortunes and very scanty ones both become rarer, every day brings the social condition of the landowner closer to that of the farmer. Neither has any natural, uncontested superiority over the other. Between two equal men, neither of them comfortable in his circumstances, the contract of hire is purely a matter of money. A man whose estate covers a whole district and who owns a hundred farms knows well how important it is to win the affections of several thousand men at once; this goal seems to demand his efforts, and he will readily make considerable sacrifices to reach it. But the man who owns a hundred acres is untouched by such considerations and cares little about winning his tenant’s private regard.

An aristocracy does not die in a single day, as a man does. The aristocratic principle is slowly undermined in people’s opinion before it is attacked in their laws. Long before open war is declared on it, one can see the tie that had held the higher classes to the lower gradually loosen. One class betrays indifference and contempt, the others jealousy and hatred; contact between rich and poor becomes less frequent and less kindly, and rents are raised. This is not the result of a democratic revolution but its sure forerunner; for an aristocracy that has lost the people’s affection, once and for all, is like a tree dead at the root, which the winds tear up the more easily the higher its branches have spread.

Over the last fifty years the rents of farms have risen amazingly, not only in France but across most of Europe. The remarkable improvements in agriculture and manufactures during the same period do not, in my opinion, suffice to explain this; one must look to another cause, more powerful and more hidden. I believe that cause lies in the democratic institutions that several European nations have adopted, and in the democratic passions that more or less stir all the rest. I have often heard great English landowners congratulate themselves that they now draw a much larger income from their estates than their fathers did. They may well have good reason to be pleased, but they certainly do not know what they are pleased about. They think they are making a clear gain, when in reality they are only making an exchange: they are giving up their influence for cash, and what they gain in money they will soon lose in power.

There is another sign by which it is easy to tell that a great democratic revolution is under way or approaching. In the Middle Ages almost all land was leased for lives or for very long terms; the household economy of that period shows that ninety-nine-year leases were then more common than twelve-year leases are now. People believed then that families were immortal. Men’s conditions seemed settled forever, and all of society seemed so fixed that no one imagined anything in its structure would ever be stirred or shaken. In ages of equality the human mind takes a different bent: the prevailing idea is that nothing lasts, and man is haunted by the thought of change. With this feeling, landowner and tenant alike instinctively dislike long terms of obligation. They fear being bound tomorrow by a contract that benefits them today. They have vague expectations of some sudden, unforeseen change in their conditions; they distrust themselves; they fear that their tastes may change, and that they will regret being unable to rid themselves of what they once coveted. Nor are these fears unfounded, for in democratic ages the most changeable thing, amid the changes all around, is the heart of man.
